common_name: Bozoisky-Select Russian Wildrye (Drought-Tolerant Perennial Cover Grass)

planting.note: Drill inoculated-not-required seed 0.5-1 inch deep at 8-10 lb per acre in late summer to fall, or very early spring in colder areas; Bozoisky-Select, released in 1984 from ARS Logan, Utah breeding work with foundation seed produced at the NRCS Bridger, Montana Plant Materials Center, is selected for superior seedling vigor from deep planting and strong drought tolerance.

directions: Drill seed shallowly into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late summer or fall so seedlings can establish a deep root system before winter; Bozoisky-Select was specifically bred for vigorous emergence even from deeper plantings than older Russian wildrye lines tolerate, making it more forgiving on dry, cloddy ground. This bunchgrass forms dense basal foliage rather than tall stems, giving it exceptional drought and cold tolerance for long-term soil cover, erosion control, and grazing on marginal dryland acreage where few other cover grasses persist. It is slow to establish in its first year but becomes a highly productive, deep-rooted perennial stand by year two or three that can be grazed, mowed, or left as permanent cover. Because it is a long-lived perennial, reserve it for dedicated soil-building or erosion-control plantings rather than a rotational annual cover crop slot.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center, Bridger, Montana

common_name: Arvika Forage Pea (Tall Long-Vined Spring Cover Crop Pea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast seed as soon as the ground can be worked in early spring at a fairly high rate; Arvika is a tall, long-vined, late-maturing forage pea with a notably durable seed coat and strong seedling vigor, commonly mixed with oats or triticale to give the weak-stemmed vines a structure to climb.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed into cool, moist soil as early in spring as the ground can be worked, since Arvika germinates well in cold soil but is a spring type rather than a true winter-hardy pea. Bred for cold-tolerant cool-season growth, it produces notably longer vines and later maturity than quicker-cycling forage peas, giving it more time to accumulate biomass when grown through a full spring season, and its tough seed coat provides better resistance to seed rot in cold, wet soil than many other pea lines. Pairing it with an oat or triticale companion keeps the sprawling vines off the ground and improves stand density and weed suppression. Mow or terminate at early flowering to maximize fixed nitrogen before the crop sets pods, since mature vines become tough and slow to break down.
sources: USDA NRCS Montana Plant Materials Technical Note: Evaluation of Cool Season Cover Crops in Southern Montana
SARE: Managing Cover Crops Profitably - Field Peas

common_name: Cinnamon Plus Red Clover (Disease-Resistant Medium Red Clover Cultivar)

planting.note: Broadcast inoculated seed at 8-10 lb per acre in late summer to fall, or frost-seed into an existing stand in late winter; Cinnamon Plus is a diploid medium red clover bred for strong resistance to northern and southern anthracnose and powdery mildew, with excellent seedling vigor for pasture renovation.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a well-prepared seedbed in late summer or fall, or frost-seed onto thin pasture or an existing grass stand in late winter so freeze-thaw cycles work the seed into the soil. Cinnamon Plus was bred with strong resistance to both northern and southern anthracnose and powdery mildew, diseases that shorten the productive life of older red clover strains, and it carries excellent seedling vigor that makes it well suited to renovating tired pastures as well as standalone cover crop stands. It fixes substantial nitrogen and holds up well under grazing or repeated mowing, regrowing vigorously after each cutting. Terminate at early bloom for peak nitrogen contribution, or allow a grazed stand to persist multiple seasons since the cultivar's disease resistance gives it better stand longevity than many older red clover types.
sources: National Alfalfa & Forage Alliance (NAAIC) variety review: Cinnamon Plus Red Clover
